entries.title: Wisconsin Democrats Ask Elections Commission to Allow Voters to Recast Absentee Ballots
entries.summary: The bipartisan panel blocked the ability to revote earlier this month after Democrat Missy Hughes exited the governor’s race.
entries.content:
Wisconsin’s gubernatorial candidates keep shuffling before next month’s primary. Now, the state Democratic party is requesting Wisconsin’s elections panel allow voters who already cast an absentee ballot to vote again.

After thousands of Wisconsinites had already submitted their absentee ballots ahead of the Aug. 11 primary, Democrats’ candidate slate shifted twice within days. Front-runner Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez ended her campaign last Friday. A day later, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley rejoined the race a week after he suspended his campaign, reentering with current Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers’ endorsement.

Earlier this month, the bipartisan Wisconsin Elections Commission blocked the ability to revote if a candidate drops out after a different Democrat, Missy Hughes, exited the governor’s race in June. Because of that ruling, Rodriguez voters and people who would have backed Crowley may have lost their chance to vote for a candidate who will actually be in the running through August, the state Democratic party argues.

Over 80,000 ballots have already been submitted, but the party argues many of these votes are going to waste due to candidates dropping or reentering the race.

The commission voted 4-2 on July 9 to issue the guidance limiting voters’ ability to “spoil” their ballots and excluded circumstances like someone deciding to vote for another candidate.

Wisconsin Democratic Party Chair Devin Remiker said “some voters will not be able to truly participate in our Democratic primary process” if the guidance is not reversed to allow new absentee ballots.

“Allowing voters to spoil and recast their ballots was standard practice in Wisconsin prior to attempts by Republicans to file frivolous lawsuits to muddy the waters,” Remiker said in a statement.

The state Democratic Party argues the new guidance should be rescinded because it reverses the commission’s own rule that was in place in 2022. It is also inconsistent with a 2006 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that stated voting rules should not be changed close to an election, they said.

In the past, Wisconsin voters were able to cancel submitted ballots and then request a new one up to three times, for any reason. But in October 2022, a county circuit judge ruled that this “ballot spoiling” practice was illegal. The 2nd District Court of Appeals reversed the 2022 ruling in February, finding that the lawsuit was not properly served.

entries.title: Mamdani Says He Can’t Arrest Netanyahu if He Comes to New York
entries.summary: The New York City mayor posted a two-minute video explaining that he does not have the authority to arrest the Israeli Prime Minister if he comes to New York City.
entries.content:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he would not arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu if he comes to New York City, a pledge he made while campaigning for mayor last year.

Netanyahu is expected to visit New York City in September for the annual United Nations General Assembly. Mamdani told The New York Times last week that he was “in active conversation” with the city’s law department over the matter, but said on Tuesday that he does not have the legal authority to enforce the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant out for Netanyahu. President Donald Trump responded to the mayor’s earlier comments in a Monday Truth Social post, saying the prime minister would not be arrested “in any way, shape or form” in the U.S.

During his mayoral campaign, Mamdani pledged to order the New York Police Department to arrest Netanyahu if he were to come to New York City. He reaffirmed his desire to do so on Tuesday in a two-minute video, calling the prime minister the “architect of a horrific genocide of the Palestinian people.”

“My administration has reviewed every avenue available under applicable law to determine whether New York City could execute the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant if Benjamin Netanyahu came here,” Mamdani said. “It is clear we do not have the independent legal authority to enforce this warrant.”

He instead turned the onus to arrest Netanyahu onto the federal government, which is unlikely to do so: “I call on them to join the ICC and execute this warrant.”

The International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024, accusing them of crimes against humanity including murder, starvation, persecution, and attacks on Gazans.

entries.title: From Cycling to Fishing, Concerns About East Potomac’s Future Go Beyond Golf
entries.summary: President Donald Trump’s plan to renovate the island park’s golf course has created an uncertain future for the area’s other public spaces.
entries.content:
Will Edwards, born and raised in southwest D.C., has been coming to East Potomac Park his entire life.

On a warm Monday evening, he and his family set up camp near Hains Point, the island park’s southern tip. They had a portable table, some chairs and some toys for Edwards’ son. A dinner of chicken and biscuits was spread out in front of them. Fishing rods hung on the fence.

“This has been a landmark for years,” Edwards said. “Years.”

Before he was married, Edwards said he used to come down here looking to meet women at social events. His wife, Carla, has different but also fond memories: as a child, she used to crawl on The Awakening, a large sculpture that was once located at Hains Point but has since moved to Maryland.

The lines from Edwards’ rods were being gently tugged by the water as he discussed the many types of fish he hoped to catch.

“Catfish, maybe a cod. Alligator gar,” he said.

Not far from the family sat a discarded container of chicken gizzards, popular bait for blue crabs.

To Carla, the park creates a sense of community.

“Most people see you fishing, they offer their bait,” she said.

But the future of these Edwards family trips to East Potomac is uncertain. The park has served as a political football in the months since President Donald Trump announced his intention to renovate the golf links at its center — an extensive project that would likely impact the entire island.

Much of the discussion in the months since has been centered on golf and golfers, but the park has a long history of recreation beyond the links. East Potomac also features tennis courts, a playground and abundant green space. Hains Point is a popular destination for picnics and weekend gatherings. In nice weather, the wide road that encircles the park is often filled with runners and bicyclists.

Hains Point recreation family (5549x3699, AR: 1.50)Early renderings of Trump’s plan seemed to spare Hains Point and other adjoining areas. But recently, Trump has been seen with new blueprints that suggest otherwise, creating a panic regarding the future of the park. On Saturday, the Washington Area Bicyclist Association hosted a rally called “Hains Point Hoopla” to raise awareness about the public amenities that could be at stake.

Trump has said he would like construction to begin in September, but his plan is certain to face red tape.

In the meantime, the park continues to serve its regulars. On Monday night, plane after plane landed at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, located directly across the water from the Edwards family. Will said any large-scale changes to the park would be “devastating.”

“This is somewhere people need to come, just to relax, despite a day,” he said. “Anybody could have a bad day, but they come here, they sit in the car, you know. Just relax.”

Earlier this month, four senators sent a letter to the Department of the Interior and the National Park Service seeking clarification on final plans for the park. The agencies are defendants in an ongoing lawsuit brought by the D.C. Preservation League and local residents, aimed at halting any proposed overhaul.

Neither the National Park Service or the Department of the Interior could be reached for comment.

This past winter, the Trump administration terminated a 50-year lease with the National Links Trust, the nonprofit tasked with managing the course. The Department of the Interior has since allowed the trust to operate the course until a “historic renovation” begins.

Torrence, who declined to give his last name because of privacy concerns, is also a District native who’s been coming to the park most of his life. Although he wasn’t aware of the proposed changes to the golf course, he has sensed more tension in the area.

“I've never had anybody ask for a fishing license down here, but now all of a sudden you have to have a fishing license, and they try to give you a citation or a ticket,” he told NOTUS. “This place was very peaceful at one point.”

Torrence said he comes to the park to “breathe life” and escape the reality of his densely populated city.

“We live in an inner city surrounded by concrete,” he said. “It's not too much wildlife out here, outdoors things you can do. So this is one of the places that a lot of inner city people come to just release.”

Many regulars admit that the park needs upgrades. Some bathrooms are out and there is overgrowth on the waterfront. The park is not perfect, but it is where they choose to spend their time.

“If anything, give it a facelift,” Torrence said. “Pick up some of these broken-down trees and stuff around there. Invest money into this place.”

entries.title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (July 24)
entries.summary: A Taylor Swift tribute band, Harry Potter Day at Nats Park, and performances across the DMV.
entries.content:
Thursday

¡Puro Ritmo! The Musical Journey of Salsa at the American History Museum
1300 Constitution Ave. NW, D.C., 10:30 a.m., free 

Located in the Molina Family Latino Gallery. Explore the rhythm, history and energy of salsa music through a guided tour. This is a bilingual multimedia exhibition presented by the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Latino.

Summer Culture Hub: Textile Techniques at Montpelier Historic Site and Museum
9650 Muirkirk Road, Laurel, MD, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., free. Through Sunday, July 26. 

Laurel’s Georgian plantation house hosts a weekend of family-friendly, hands-on crafting workshops. Learn about historic textile arts that would have been practiced by both enslaved artisans and wealthy landowners at this event run by the Maryland National-Capital Park and Planning Commission.

Girl Scouts block party at Franklin Park
1332 I St. NW, D.C., 6:30 p.m., free

Enjoy sweet treats and dance the night away to Be'la Dona, an all-women group performing live go-go music. There will also be food vendors, face paintings, glitter tattoos, nail art and other interactive activities for all ages.

More to explore:
Analog Dinner Nights: Mahjong! at Flor Coffee + Books
Board Game Speed Dating at Dacha Beer Garden (Shaw)

Friday

Rock the Dock: A Taylor Swift tribute at The Wharf 
970 Wharf St. SW, D.C., 7 p.m., free

Every Friday night at the Transit Pier, enjoy free live music next to the water. This Friday, The Fearless Eras, a Taylor Swift tribute band, will be playing all the hits. All ages are welcome, as are dogs on leashes, and enjoying food from the Wharf’s many restaurants is encouraged.

Pianist Joyce Yang with the Baltimore Symphony at the Music Center at Strathmore
5301 Tuckerman Lane, North Bethesda, MD, 7:30 p.m., $35 to $112 (second show Saturday)

In early 1800s Italy, rumor had it that violinist Niccolò Paganini sold his soul to the devil in exchange for virtuosic talents. A century later, Russian composer Sergei Rachmaninoff arranged one of Paginini’s signature motifs into his fiendishly difficult “Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini.” Pianist Joyce Yang takes the devil down to Strathmore, with Lidiya Yankovskaya in the conductor’s seat.

Candlelight: ’90s Hip-Hop on Strings at National City Christian Church
5 Thomas Circle NW, 6:45 p.m., $63.50 to $100

Prefer your Snoop Dogg played by a string quartet? Fever, the national event presenter that curates romantic musical evenings outside of traditional concert halls, has arranged a memory-lane playlist including Lauryn Hill, the Notorious B.I.G. and the Wu Tang Clan, to be performed by the Listeso String Quartet.

Rooted in Resistance dinner at the Festival Center
1640 Columbia Road NW, D.C., 7 p.m., $50 to $100

Enjoy Palestinian food, art and performance at the dinner that kicks off the Rooted in Resistance: Here Eternally festival weekend, organized by the Museum of the Palestinian People. Alongside dinner, guests can experience live music, spoken word, dance, art and a moderated panel, with proceeds supporting the museum.

More to explore:
Jazz in the Garden at the National Gallery of Art Sculpture Garden
D.C’s Best comedy showcase at Hotbed

Saturday

Poet Life Fest at Gateway DC pavilion 
2700 Martin Luther King Jr. Ave. SE, D.C., Noon, free

Part of a weeklong lineup of events, Poet Life Fest is a family-friendly, daylong experience for attendees to enjoy performances of poetry and music, plus vendors, food trucks and community.

Harry Potter Day at Nationals Park
1500 South Capitol St. SE, D.C., 4:05 p.m.

As the Washington Nationals play the Arizona Diamondbacks, Nationals Park will transform into Hogwarts for Harry Potter Day. There will be a themed photo booth, face painters, balloon artists, caricaturists and a potion-making station.

“Pippin” at Signature Theatre
4200 Campbell Ave., Arlington, VA, 8 p.m.

Signature Theatre will stage its final showings of “Pippin,” a coming-of-age musical with music and lyrics by Stephen Schwartz. A traveling troupe of performers takes the audience through the story of Pippin, the restless heir of Charlemagne, on his quest for purpose.

More to explore:
“The Sound of Music” screening at the National Gallery of Art
“CrazySexyCool” matinee at Arena Stage (includes child care)
Ringside wrestling at Anthem Row

Sunday

District Vibes at Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library
901 G St. NW, D.C., 1 p.m., free (through Sept. 27) 

The Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library is celebrating America’s 250th birthday with “District Vibes / American Pride: How D.C. Changed American Culture.” The exhibit focuses on the contributions of D.C. to America, from the football hurdle to the modern blood bank.

More to explore:
District Fringe at the University of District Columbia
Piña Colada Festival at Colada Shop

entries.title: Suspicion and Doubt at the National Civics Contest
entries.summary: America’s finest young scholars competed to mark their country's birthday. It led to a disputed finish in the age of mistrust.
entries.content:
The morning after the competition, Aangad Singh's family was trying to figure out what went wrong. They were walking through the National Museum of Natural History, going over answers, doing the math.

“It doesn’t make sense,” said his mother, Ramandeep.

Ramandeep was good at numbers. But she couldn’t make them explain how her 15-year-old son had missed the top three in the Presidential 1776 Award competition, the civics contest for high schoolers that President Donald Trump’s party planners had created to celebrate America’s 250th birthday. She had watched the first round, when the field was whittled from 20 to eight, and the second round, when it went from eight to three. There was celebrity host Mario Lopez, an exclusive broadcast deal with CBS and a Kennedy Center stage that mixed game show spectacle with civic pageantry. The only thing missing was a scoreboard.

She told herself not to complain. She didn’t want to be that mom, a sore loser whose kid could never fail. On their way out, though, other parents kept stopping them.

“Shocked,” said more than one.

Later, a boy stopped her and said a group of contestants had kept score themselves.

“We thought he won,” the boy said.

She approached an official from the Department of Education, which had helped run the contest, and asked for the final scores.

“Proprietary,” the official said.

In the museum, Ramandeep furrowed her brow.

“How did they count the numbers?” she said. “That’s something we need to understand.”

“We can only find out when they telecast it,” said her husband, Bhalindar.

Ramandeep pursed her lips. The broadcast was three weeks away.
0173-S3410642-260609- ©Doug Coulter (1).jpg (4200x2362, AR: 1.78)It wasn’t like them to feel skeptical. She and Bhalindar were Indian immigrants whose trust in the American system had led to degrees, careers and citizenship. They bought a four-bedroom Colonial in a quiet Connecticut city and sent their kids to public school. They passed their faith in the United States down to Aangad, who won awards for his speeches about the country’s founding ideals. But now they, like so many others, were wondering whether the game was rigged.

It was a reluctant half-step into the age of suspicion. The U.S. was just one of many democratic nations riding the same wave of paranoia, with polls showing trust in major institutions at or near all-time lows. In America, the president questioned whether the elections were free and fair as citizens sank deeper into the embrace of their tribes. The world’s leading deepfake expert told The New York Times that he no longer trusted his own eyes, that our whole visual system was on the verge of collapse. And just as the Singhs were walking the halls of the museum, senators and Trump judicial appointees on Capitol Hill were sparring over the results of a presidential election that happened six years ago.

Aangad’s parents didn’t want to accuse anyone of fixing the competition. But they felt compelled to ask questions because their son never would. When his mother had dropped him off for his first day of kindergarten, he did not cry, even though she could tell he wanted to. For years the story served as a tidy summation of her son, a rule follower who hid his emotions, an intellectual who didn’t mind having more books than friends. But at some point she had figured out how to tell he was upset: He would take little sips of water over and over again.

Shortly after noon, the Singhs left the museum and went to a café. When Aangad opened the door, he ran into the blond girl from Wyoming, Miriam Washut, who he was pretty sure had won the whole thing. She must be headed to the White House for the special tour of the Oval Office, he thought.

Her father, wearing a black cowboy hat, stuck out his hand.

“You did extremely well,” he said.

“Thank you,” Aangad said.
P20260610MR-0333 (1) copy.jpg (3000x1688, AR: 1.78)Aangad turned to Miriam, whose eyes dropped to the floor. Her voice pitched up. She waved her hands at her sides.

“That was insane,” she said. “You clearly knew everything.”

Aangad nodded, face blank, and Miriam’s family went on their way.

Aangad walked over to his parents’ table.

“What did she say?” his father asked.

“That I should have won,” Aangad said.

No one said anything for a long time.

Aangad took a small sip of water.

* * *

Three weeks later, Aangad’s family took positions in the living room. His dad was on one couch, laptop open to a spreadsheet titled “1776_Broadcast_Audit.” His mother was on the edge of the other couch, drumming her right foot like a kick pedal. Aangad was between them, lying on a recliner with his feet up, talking quietly to his little sister. On the side table was a black metal water bottle. He had just filled it.

They were at his uncle’s house in suburban Toronto, where they vacationed every year. Ramandeep and her brother had grown up on a farm in India. They didn't go back much; they liked how little their kids knew about homesteading. Now, the siblings were competing to see who could own the biggest house in North America, and her brother, a hardware engineer, was winning. Ramandeep had done everything to help her kids get ahead, too, including giving them names that started with two As in part so they'd always be first in alphabetical lists at school.
SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM017 copy.jpg (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM055 copy.jpg (7545x5030, AR: 1.50)“It began online with the Impossible Civics Test,” Mario Lopez said on TV, and everyone in the room stopped talking.

CBS didn’t show the round of 20. And it cut the opening speech from Education Secretary Linda McMahon.

“There is hope for the next 50 years that the flame of liberty still burns bright in the next generation,” she had said. "The great American story is still being written by you.”

They’d hoped the broadcast would include a live scoreboard, so they could see where things went wrong. But the first segment sped by without one.

“Why aren’t they showing scores?” his uncle asked.

Then the second segment sped by too.

“What’s the score?” Aangad said, looking at his dad.

“I don’t know,” his dad said. The show was going too fast and the commentary in the living room was too loud for him to keep up.

Aangad knew he’d been behind at this point. He’d won the buzzer race only once in eight questions. But the final two segments were far more valuable, and he knew he’d done well.

On TV, Mario Lopez introduced the third segment: Each contestant would stand alone at the lectern to answer a multipart question about the U.S. Constitution. Then each of the five judges would grade it.
SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM086 copy.jpg (7065x4710, AR: 1.50)Aangad watched the contestants.

The boy from Michigan got a full 20 points.

The girl from Washington did too.

So did the girl from Wyoming.

“According to Article 3 of the U.S. Constitution, in which cases do the federal courts have jurisdiction?” the proctor said to Aangad on TV. “List at least four for full credit.”

As he answered, little summary boxes popped up on screen.

“Maritime jurisdiction.” Green.

“Parties of state and citizens of another state.” Red.

“What?” Aangad said on the couch, his voice sharp.

He got two more green boxes, then another red: “Case with state and foreign nation.”

“What?” he said again. He handed his dad his phone. He’d pulled up the Constitution and highlighted a paragraph with the phrases “between a State and Citizens of another State” and “between a State, or the Citizens thereof, and foreign States, Citizens or Subjects.”

“Read this, read this, read this, read this right now,” Aangad said.

His dad read it. “It’s within the Constitution,” he said.
SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM038 copy.jpg (6000x2968, AR: 2.02)At the end of the segment, a scoreboard flashed onscreen.

Michigan was first with 23 points.

Aangad was sixth with 16.

He took a sip from his water bottle.

“They just made this whole thing for show,” his uncle said. “They know who they want to win.”

The final challenge was a lightning round. Each contestant had 30 seconds to answer as many questions as possible, and each correct answer was worth two points.

Michigan got 10 right.

Washington, 10.

Wyoming, 10.

Then Aangad came to the stage.

The first question flashed on the monitor: “Which amendment ended slavery?”

Aangad answered. Incorrect.

“Thirteenth!” Aangad cried on the couch. “I said Thirteenth!”

After that, TV Aangad started flying. All the nights he and his dad had practiced the lightning round were paying off. He processed questions nearly instantly and answered almost without thinking. The screen said +2, +2, +2.
SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM097 copy.jpg (4100x2733, AR: 1.50)Aangad got one more wrong. But watching from the couch, he didn’t protest. He saw now the judges had wanted a more technical answer.

In the end, the judges marked 12 answers correct. Aangad concluded they must have thought he pronounced thirteenth like fourteenth. “I say that THirteenth like an ‘F’ sound.” Later, he’d feel validated when he realized the auto-generated subtitles said “thirteenth.”

Before Mario Lopez revealed the top three, he walked around the stage and interviewed every contestant. Aangad gave a polished answer about being proud to share his knowledge of the nation’s founding principles. The girl from Washington was brought to tears again. A boy from Arizona said winning would mean everything: “I’ve always wanted to meet the man, the myth, the legend — Donald Trump!”

After the finalists were announced, Aangad watched Michigan, Washington and Wyoming take center stage.

On TV, he calmly applauded. On the couch, he picked up his water bottle and took a big gulp.
SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM068 copy.jpg (7914x5276, AR: 1.50)
* * *

Aangad’s family watched the rest of the program in relative quiet. Miriam from Wyoming won, just as Aangad had suspected, and then the finalists took a trip to the White House.

They stood by the Resolute Desk, a snapshot of Trump’s education agenda. Miriam was homeschooled. The boy from Michigan attended a private Catholic school. The girl from Washington, who went to public school, had told CNN that she supported Trump and believed the most important thing was “everyone walking away from the competition knowing this is the greatest country of the world.”

In the Oval Office, she told the president she wanted to go to Hillsdale College.

“Hillsdale?” Aangad’s father said.

“Republican college,” Aangad reminded him. They’d been on campus in Michigan last month for the American Legion’s National Oratorical Contest. The school had donated $10 million to the president’s Freedom 250 committee and helped develop its history programs.

“I can give you a recommendation,” the president said to the girl. “I think we should get you in.”
SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM104 (1) copy.jpg (4510x4510, AR: 1.00)The finalists left with two commemorative coins, one of which said “THE FINAL MISSION,” a reference to the education secretary’s promise to “sunset a 46-year-old, $3 trillion failed federal education bureaucracy in Washington, D.C.”

Then the broadcast ended.

“You could have been there,” Aangad’s father said.

Everyone let his words hang in the air.

* * *

Over a late dinner of curry chicken, two factions began to form. Aangad and his father thought the judges must just be incompetent or mistaken. Aangad’s mother and uncle suspected a conspiracy: Someone had not wanted the brown kid in the turban to represent the youth of America in the Oval Office. His uncle advised them to go directly to the Education Department.

“The whole point is to initiate the investigation,” he said.

“They may have some kind of intention that these people shouldn’t be there,” his mother said.

“You don’t know that,” Aangad replied. “You’re just assuming.”

Aangad spooned out more chicken and rice.

“I personally think that they just had faulty sources,” he said. Discussion turned to the five judges. They were all teachers from across the country who were past recipients of the prestigious James Madison Memorial Fellowship to study the Constitution. At least three of them must have mistakenly graded the constitutional answers as incorrect, Aangad said, and it seemed likely to him that they hadn’t memorized Article 3 as well as he had. Or maybe his answers didn’t match the phrasing on their rubrics.

“That shows ineptness,” he said.

After tiramisu, Ramandeep made an impassioned case for justice. She didn’t care about the share of $250,000 in scholarship money, she said. She wanted recognition for Aangad’s hard work. And if the system really was biased, they had to fight on behalf of every kid who could be hurt by it.
SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM107 copy.jpg (7237x4825, AR: 1.50)“But we don’t know if it’s systemic,” Bhalindar replied. He defended trusting the system, trusting the nation’s founding documents, which he had devoted hours to helping their son study. A few bad judges don’t undermine an entire system.

Aangad’s uncle had gone to bed. Aangad was on the couch, eyes closed.

If they made a strong case, Bhalindar said, maybe the Education Department would admit its mistake. Ramandeep doubted they’d even get a response.

She was equally pessimistic that they could get anywhere by filing a lawsuit.

“We will not be able to afford to fight against the system.”

On that point, Bhalindar had to agree.

The best strategy, Ramandeep said, was media attention. They could present their findings and let the public decide.

"That's your power," she said, turning to me.

This was uncomfortable. Weeks earlier, as I looked for a way to write about America’s 250th, the Education Department had recommended I reach out to the Singhs. I then followed Aangad through the competition, not knowing if he would even advance.

Now, their predicament felt like a window into something bigger: If the government or the courts couldn’t bring them justice, then maybe, they thought, the media could. All I could do was write what happened. But the Fourth Estate was another institution at low ebbs in trust and influence, and Bhalindar knew it. He doubted the government would bow to media pressure.

“At least our story is in front of the public,” Ramandeep said. “That’s our closure.”

“‘Closure’ is the right word,” Bhalindar said, and just before midnight, all out of words, he reassured his wife that they would figure this out together. She gave him a tired smile and went upstairs.

Bhalindar sat on the couch for a while and looked at the dark TV.

* * *

The only way to know whether the system was fair was to test it.

So, back home in Connecticut, Bhalindar used a chatbot to find lawyers with experience in federal education, federal agencies and administrative law.

“Dear Counsel,” he wrote to them, “I am seeking a confidential initial consultation regarding a potential dispute.”

He attached a packet of evidence that included their calculation of the final scores.

Michigan, 43.

Wyoming, 42.

Washington, 41.

Aangad, 40.

If either of Aangad’s “incorrect” answers had been scored correctly, his father argued, he would’ve finished in the top three.

“I am looking for counsel who can objectively evaluate the facts, advise on preservation of evidence and procedure, and determine whether there is a viable legal or administrative path forward,” Bhalindar wrote.

Aangad moved on. He followed the U.S. in the World Cup and enjoyed fireworks on the Fourth of July. He didn’t see Miriam, the girl from Wyoming, tell her local newspaper that she was surprised by who made the top three. He didn’t see the Education Department use Miriam’s homeschooling as a cudgel in the culture war.

His dad would email the Department of Education to ask for a review, and then ask again, and hear nothing back. His belief in the system would remain steadfast, though he’d wish someone would acknowledge his requests. The Education Department would tell NOTUS that the competition questions were “developed, judged, and scored independently by the James Madison Memorial Fellowship Foundation.” The foundation would not respond to a detailed list of questions.

Meanwhile, Aangad focused on the future. He made videos about public speaking and wrote a speech about Sikhism and looked into the U.S. Senate Youth Program. He geared up for junior year and tried to figure out what to study in college. Law, maybe? Anything but medicine, for sure; blood made him queasy. But first, he would accept an award from the Connecticut American Legion. His winning speech had focused on the dangers of civic ignorance.

As long as people have the power to make choices, he said, democracies are a series of infinite crossroads. The Constitution, the Bill of Rights, the Federalist Papers — they embody these crossroads. And on the nation's 250th anniversary, Aangad urged his fellow Americans to choose to learn their history before a tyrant defined their rights for them.

He stood in a suit at a lectern at the front of a ballroom. The audience was mostly old, white men, but the traditional American Legion caps they wore were shaped like Aangad’s red turban.
20260517_Connecticut_Aangad Singh_JAB3324 copy.jpg (5001x3334, AR: 1.50)Aangad told the crowd his favorite article in the Constitution was Article 3, Section 3, which in three sentences established a high bar for what could be considered treason against the United States.

“It truly is extraordinary how our founders had incredible foresight, and the various methods to which our Constitution attempts to integrate its people into government,” he said.

The people applauded. Aangad stepped back and nodded. He hadn’t brought any water with him. He didn’t need it now.

entries.title: USDA Workers Don’t Plan to Stay on the Job as Offices Relocate
entries.summary: Employees say the moves are backdoor layoffs that will hamper policy, research and wildfire response.
entries.content:
Workers at the Department of Agriculture are trying to stop mandatory relocations, which they warned are mass layoffs in disguise.

Employees throughout the department told NOTUS their colleagues overwhelmingly did not plan to move to new offices across the country. This month, employee unions and nonprofit organizations asked a federal judge to halt the USDA’s plans.

Their warnings: A reduction in force at this scale will delay policy changes, damage research, slow getting federal dollars out the door and hamper wildfire response.

“No one was asking for this,” former USDA Undersecretary Robert Bonnie told NOTUS. “It’s hard to reach any other conclusion than that the purpose of this is to dramatically reduce the size of the federal civil service. There’s no compelling reason to do this.”

It’s potentially another drastic reduction in the USDA’s workforce, which already faced some of the most significant cuts during the DOGE era.

In a 2025 workforce plan made public this month as part of the employee groups’ ongoing lawsuit, USDA said it was anticipating that “a significant number of employees will decline geographic reassignments” out of Washington and regional and state offices.

“We absolutely do view it as a RIF in disguise,” one employee at the Foreign Agricultural Service, USDA’s trade policy arm, told NOTUS, using an abbreviation for the term reduction in force.

In multiple polls from various unions representing USDA employees, around 80% say they would rather quit than move. It’s a percentage that would exceed the loss of staff in 2019, when the USDA moved hundreds of employees from its Economic Research Service and National Institute of Food and Agriculture offices in Washington to Kansas City, Missouri.

Following that move, both agencies lost more than half of their workforces and subsequent reviews by the Government Accountability Office found they spent years recovering from the significant losses in productivity.

The USDA is once again moving employees from both agencies to Kansas City, as it did in Trump’s first term, after former President Joe Biden brought most staff back to Washington. Kansas City will serve as one of the five regional hubs USDA is building around the country, with others in Utah, North Carolina, Colorado and Indiana.

The department last year announced it would push 2,600 employees out of Washington, while also consolidating regional offices around the country. It has so far announced new locations for a dozen of its subagencies, though in most cases it has yet to issue assignments for individual employees.

USDA officials have said the changes will put employees closer to the farmers and ranchers they serve, though only around 10% of the USDA workforce is currently in the Washington region. The department did not respond to questions from NOTUS, instead pointing to a tweet from USDA Undersecretary Stephen Vaden noting it is proceeding as scheduled with relocations.

A former longtime senior USDA employee expressed concern that the first employees to leave will be the agency’s most skilled and longest-tenured staff, as they have the most options to work somewhere else, creating a brain drain in the department.

“If you don’t have options, you’re more likely to take the move,” the former employee told NOTUS.

USDA has shed 21,000 employees since Trump took office. The department has shifted away from its original plan to follow up last year’s incentivized attrition with mass layoffs, but employees suggested the relocations will have the same effect.

In declarations filed in court and interviews, employees described how a change in office would alter their lives, since they own property in their current locations, their spouses have jobs there, or they would have to leave their support system and start a new life in a new state.

“They’ve got families,” one USDA employee said. “They don’t want to uproot their lives.”

At some components, such as the U.S. Forest Service, which is moving its headquarters to Salt Lake City and closing most of its regional offices and many of its research stations, management has openly told employees they expect the relocations to result in significant attrition.

USDA sent about a third of FAS civil service staff based in D.C. letters Friday telling them that they’re relocating to Kansas City. Much of the work involves coordinating with foreign embassies and the State Department, so the move “doesn’t make any sense,” the employee said. The agency has already lost more than a quarter of its staff.

USDA employees have also expressed concern the department will target specific people for moves. “We believe they’re going to use this opportunity to try to move key, long-term employees to try to get them out,” one Natural Resources Conservation Service employee said.

Workers are also sounding the alarm on the impacts that relocations will have, both as a result of an accompanying brain drain and the lack of concentration for remaining staff.

“We’re literally going to be not able to do things on time,” the NRCS employee said. “We’ll be doing things improperly.”

Employees throughout the USDA warned that headquarters and regional engineers who help standardize policy across the country are set to leave in droves rather than move, which will lead to slower policy rollouts, inconsistent implementation of department rules and more litigation that will delay timber sales and other administration priorities.

“We basically have to rebuild that expertise from a technical standpoint,” another Forest Service employee said.

In a recent presentation to agency leadership, employees in the Agricultural Research Service warned of the consequences of closing down the famed Beltsville Agricultural Research Center in Maryland and dispersing its projects around the country. The facility is sending its pollinator bee laboratory to Fargo, North Dakota, for example.

“We mostly made the case that invaluable resources would be lost,” one ARS employee said. “And that the program moving there would not be able to complete their mission.”

The Forest Service has stressed that its cadre of firefighters will not be affected by the changes, but employees have cautioned that incident management teams, which the agency stands up for major fires, are made up of non-firefighter staff still subject to relocations. The agency has already shed 15% of its workforce under Trump, and further reductions resulting from upcoming changes would exacerbate shortfalls as the agency seeks to provide logistical support to fire crews.

“We are going to see, if we haven’t already, impacts to our wildfire response,” one regional Forest Service employee said.

The complaints have largely fallen on deaf ears.

At several components, the department first aims to send senior staff to new locations while the rest of the workforce awaits its fate. Very few of those top career officials plan to move, employees said.

The delays in information for those remaining has added anxiety and confusion, they said, especially after earlier this year top officials said everyone would have their new assignments and be moved by the end of the summer so they could have their kids enrolled for the start of the 2026 school year. At least some senior executives have told staff they cannot share more information because they have signed non-disclosure agreements related to the reorganization.

“Everything they say, the targets they want to meet, they blow by them and then they don’t acknowledge they’ve blown by them,” the NRCS employee said. “It doesn’t inspire confidence. They’re not doing anything they said they would do.”

The overall plan appears to still be in flux. Regional Forest Service employees in Portland, Oregon, for example, were told this week that they would not be shipped to other cities and that the agency had instead found office space for them at various buildings within 50 miles of their current duty stations. The Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, currently battling the New World Screwworm outbreak, has told staff they would not be moved, though new hiring will occur at hub locations.

The new organizational chart of the newly renamed Food and Nutrition Administration isn’t expected to be fully implemented until mid-2027, the acting head of the component told staff last week in an email, viewed by NOTUS, that acknowledged “for many of you, there are still more questions than answers.”

The agency also recently agreed not to move union-eligible staff currently working in Alexandria, Virginia, outside of the Washington region until 2029 “in the interest of maintaining workforce stability during periods of attrition,” according to a memorandum of understanding with the union obtained by NOTUS.

USDA had faced particularly significant pushback on the FNA moves from lawmakers who decried potential disruptions to nutrition programs like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Women, Infants and Children Program.

Only about a third of the staff in FNA work in the D.C. region, however, and others still don’t know where they’ll be relocated. Most have voiced opposition to the move.

“My team is of the opinion that, like, the program [SNAP] would fall apart,” said another FNA employee, who is leaving the agency over the potential moves. The employee said there would be insufficient staff to assist states and that Trump administration efforts to reform the program “would go down the toilet.”

Federal employee unions and nonprofits have asked a federal judge in San Francisco to temporarily block the Trump administration from reorganizing or downsizing any USDA agency. That motion seeks to stop the closing, moving or consolidating of offices, or transferring programs between offices, and to stop USDA from sending any further relocation notices or removing employees who already declined to move.

In a filing in the case, the unions argue in part the relocations conflict with spending legislation. USDA initially sought congressional authorization for its downsizing and reorganization plans as part of its fiscal 2026 budget request, but lawmakers rejected the proposed cuts and included language in the approved spending plan barring USDA from using appropriated funds to move offices without congressional approval.

USDA management has requested such permission on a rolling basis for each of its components, but has indicated it will not wait for an explicit sign-off before moving forward.

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins has defended the relocations as a management improvement rather than a workforce-reduction tactic, telling lawmakers at a House Agriculture Committee hearing last month that moving staff outside Washington would be a “massive value add” for USDA’s research operations because “we have some extraordinary researchers, but most of them don’t want to be in Washington, D.C.”

Employees rejected that argument.

“Based on the fact that they moved near every single office,” one Forest Service employee said of the workforce reduction efforts, “yeah that seems like the goal.”

entries.title: Smithsonian Showdown
entries.content:
Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: The Smithsonian under scrutiny, Carter Barron’s (temporary) return and a fresh look at the Commanders’ stadium plans.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.


THE LATEST

Republican lawmakers grilled the director of the Smithsonian’s U.S. history museum yesterday over concerns the institution is too “woke.”

The two-hour hearing was the latest installment in President Donald Trump’s “ongoing review” of the Smithsonian and his continued effort to remake Washington and its cultural institutions.

Representatives took aim at several exhibits, including ones on slavery, the American entertainment industry and girls going through puberty, NOTUS’ Eric Katz reports.

“History is incredibly challenging and … if we tell it in its richness, we absolutely, I think, have objects that can make people uncomfortable,” director Anthea Hartig fired back.

There are signs of life in Rock Creek Park, despite the cultural climate. Carter Barron Amphitheater, the park’s 76-year-old outdoor venue that has been shuttered and in disrepair for a decade, will host a three-night concert series in August featuring jazz, gospel and go-go. But this isn’t a permanent reopening. Carter Barron still needs significant work, and a local effort to upgrade the iconic site is ongoing.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Trump’s plans to renovate the golf links at East Potomac Park could affect the park’s other public spaces, worrying everyone from cyclists to fishers, NOTUS’ Shamira Muhammad reports.

Metro wants automated doors on Red Line platforms to be installed as part of a $913 million modernization project, ABC7 reports.

D.C. firefighters will get higher wages after their union reached a new collective bargaining agreement with the District yesterday, following nearly two years of contentious negotiations. They’ll receive a 3.5% increase next fiscal year and retroactive 2% and 3.5% increases for the 2025 and 2026 fiscal years, too.

“Like everybody else, we're all struggling with higher utility bills, elevated grocery prices, you name it,” the union’s president, David Hoagland, told NOTUS. “It's a much-needed increase at a time when affordability is [at] the top of everybody's mind.”





FROM VIRGINIA

A new Virginia law extending the grace period for paying rent to 14 days is just one of the tenant protection policies being rolled out by the state, the Virginia Mercury reports.





FROM MARYLAND

Marylanders are fighting back against data centers and getting results, WAMU reports. Montgomery and Prince George’s counties have paused the development of new data centers, and one state senator told WAMU they may propose a statewide moratorium this summer.





PLAN YOUR WEEKEND


For the Swiftie: Rock the Dock: A Taylor Swift tribute at The Wharf, Friday.

For the Potterhead: Harry Potter Day at Nationals Park, Saturday.

For the history buff: District Vibes at Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library, ongoing.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

Commanders stadium updated rendering (2538x1334, AR: 1.90)Check out this fresh rendering of the new Commanders stadium. Buried in a recent presentation to the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts is one of the first comprehensive views of what the new stadium will look like for most fans approaching from the west, including what’s being called Festival Plaza and the residential and retail development that will frame one side of it. There’s lots more to dig through here.

Congratulate AJ Dybantsa on a new position. More young athletes are opting for LinkedIn as their social media of choice, The Banner reports, using the buttoned-up, business-centric platform as a way to connect with fans without sharing too much. The Wizards rookie has gotten in on the trend, posting last month that he was starting a new full-time role as “Professional Basketball Player.”

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals at Rockies, 3:10 p.m. (MLB.TV)

WNBA: Mystics vs. Aces, 7:30 p.m. (Monumental)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photo from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts. One last thing: that three-bedroom house with a pool we showed you yesterday is located in Virginia, and 36% of you guessed that right. The most common guess was Maryland.

entries.title: ‘Beautifully Messy’
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Big day in the House for big bills. A must-read civics lesson. Don’t put too much stock in the stock-banning push. DHS has a contract to buy body-worn cameras. And: A top DHS official investing like a Democrat.

THE LATEST

What the president’s watching: House Republicans are about to bolt for August recess, and thus have a make-it-or-break-it day to push through a litany of White House priorities they can deploy as fodder on the campaign trail. Donald Trump put on a charm offensive in the Oval Office last night, a source familiar with the meeting told NOTUS’ Kadia Goba, sending a dozen of his allies back to the Capitol with signed baseball hats and a nudge to deliver on his agenda.

The remaining question is whether the House GOP conference will be able to get it all done before members depart this week, and if the Senate, which is sticking around for at least another week, will go along — or if they’ll all go home empty-handed.

“We’re dead set on fulfilling our role in this partnership with our president,” Rep. Clay Higgins (R-Louisiana) told Manuela, calling the final legislative lift and Senate negotiations “beautifully messy right now.”

Already done: The House passed the government funding stopgap 220-205 last night.

Left on the plate: A must-pass defense policy bill, as well as the $95 billion budget blueprint for the Iran war, farm aid and parts of Trump’s voting-restrictions bill.

The problem for House members is twofold. First, they don’t know what the Senate will do with these bills — especially the supplemental measure with portions of the SAVE America Act that are DOA in the upper chamber right now. (Senate Majority Leader John Thune also said yesterday that the White House has a different plan for the stopgap than the House’s.) And second, spending large sums of money and the war with Iran aren’t popular talking points back home.

Adding it all up: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth finally offered a preliminary price tag for the war in a tense back-and-forth with senators yesterday. Hegseth said the war will cost taxpayers nearly $38 billion by the end of September — though experts last month had already estimated its cost to be roughly $40 billion, and that’s before the ceasefire collapsed and daily strikes resumed, NOTUS’ Joe Gould and Hamed Ahmadi report.

Open tabs: A Houthi Blockade Could Worsen an Already Fragile Oil Market (NYT); Software Glitch Put Thousands of Noncitizens on New Jersey Voter Rolls (NOTUS); Zelensky ousts Ukraine’s military commander as major shake-up continues (WaPo); Trump Approves Landmark Nuclear Deal With Saudi Arabia (WSJ)

THE BIG ONE

A civics lesson: Aangad Singh and his family left Washington in June with no trophy but a lot of questions. They believe Aangad correctly answered nearly every single question in the Presidential 1776 Award civics competition, and yet he didn’t even finish in the top three.

“It doesn’t make sense,” his mother, Ramandeep Singh, told NOTUS’ Sam Fortier for a dizzying, spellbinding story about doubts and distrust in our age of suspicion.

The prospect that the Department of Education may have fixed the competition and a chorus of validation from Aangad’s fellow contestants shook his immigrant family, who strongly believe in American ideals, to the core. So they went searching for answers, and recourse, not knowing what they might find.

From the campaign trail


Michigan money: Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign raised $3.3 million in just three weeks, with 68% of donors giving to his camp for the first time, according to numbers his campaign shared exclusively with NOTUS’ Daniella Diaz. El-Sayed will face off against Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Aug. 4 Democratic primary.

From the Hill

What ban? After an exhausting few months of legislative sausage making, the House is finally set to vote today on a bill that would restrict stock trading by members of Congress. Curtailing lawmakers’ ability to profit off of individual stock has been a longtime priority for some members. However, it’s not a safe bet it’ll make it through the Senate, NOTUS’ Avani Kalra and Taylor Giorno report.

House Republicans have tied the stock-trading ban to a bill that would require proof of citizenship to register to vote and voter identification to cast a ballot — two issues the Senate lacks the votes to pass. A second reason? The Senate hasn’t even scheduled it.

“We have a whole list of things that we’re going to talk about on how to prioritize, because it takes a lot more time in the Senate to get things done,” Sen. John Barrasso (R-Wyoming), the Republican whip, told reporters.

From the administration

Body-worn cameras on the way? The Department of Homeland Security ordered more than $30 million in body cameras from Axon Enterprise after recent fatal shootings by federal immigration agents, NOTUS’ Jackie Llanos reports — from contracts awarded just days ago.

DHS has already spent millions on body cameras, but immigration agents weren’t wearing them at the time of the shootings in Maine and Texas.

Not moving: The Department of Agriculture announced in July 2025 that it was reorganizing, a mammoth project that would relocate more than half of its D.C. workforce and other employees around the country. Critics argued it could be a sneaky way to lay people off. Now a year later, workers say they don’t want to move and the shake-up would severely hurt the department, NOTUS’ Tyler Spence, Eric Katz and Natalie Alms report.

Employees are sounding the alarm: policy rollouts, damage research, wildfire response and getting money out the door will all be delayed, they say, if the workforce is significantly diminished.

ON NOTUS PODCAST

From your favorite podcast app: On today’s episode of On NOTUS, Rep. Jim Himes (D-Connecticut) warned that Trump could interfere in November’s midterm elections and urged Americans to think through the president’s election claims. “If an individual citizen can’t exercise the critical faculties involved in seeing the president’s lies for what they are, if 50% of America believes lies that are easily disprovable, we’re done,” Himes told NOTUS’ Kadia Goba, though he added that he wasn’t pessimistic about voters. He also discussed the fight over FISA, his belief in a “big tent” Democratic Party, his beekeeping hobby and what Congress has in common with a jar of bees.

NOTUS METRO

NOTUS has some of the best reporters covering D.C.-area news, sports and culture. Sign up for our local newsletter!

Local news: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend, by Torrie Herrington

From Cycling to Fishing, Concerns About East Potomac’s Future Go Beyond Golf, by Shamira Muhammad

NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

The secretary of defense is offering hormone replacement therapy for warfighters with low testosterone. But his Senate testimony yesterday left Dana Milbank wondering: Does Pete Hegseth have too much?

NEW ON NOTUS

Stocking up: A top DHS official is intentionally investing his money like a congressional Democrat, according to his federal financial disclosures reviewed by NOTUS’ Dave Levinthal. Pedro M. Allende, a department under secretary, recently purchased between $15,001 and $50,000 worth of shares in an exchange-traded fund that mimics moves made by Democratic members of Congress.

Dan Weiskopf, the senior portfolio manager for the group that oversees the ETF, told Dave it is an “inherent conflict of interest” for someone in Allende’s role to invest in the fund.

More: Trump Lifts the Ban on Direct U.S. Flights to Lebanon, by Jenna Monnin

Cleo Fields Won’t Seek Reelection After Redistricting in Louisiana, by Torrie Herrington

Mamdani Says He Can’t Arrest Netanyahu if He Comes to New York, by Manuela Silva

Wisconsin Dems Ask Elections Commission to Allow Voters to Recast Absentee Ballots, by Torrie Herrington

NOT US

  • The Secretary of Homeland, by Nick Miroff for The Atlantic
  • The New York Young Republican Club Has an Antisemitism Problem, by Nathan Taylor Pemberton for New York magazine
  • How the G.O.P. Turned Olive Garden Into a Voter ID Talking Point, by Michael Gold for The New York Times

Thank you for reading! If you liked this edition of the NOTUS Newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If this newsletter was shared with you, please sign up — it’s free! Have a tip? Email us at tips@notus.com. And as always, we’d love to hear your thoughts at newsletters@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Thomas Burr, Brett Bachman and Andrew Burton. Photo by Mark Schiefelbein/AP.

entries.title: Jim Himes Sounds the Alarm on Potential Trump Interference in the Midterms
entries.summary: The top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee warns against how that interference could play out.
entries.content:
Rep. Jim Himes said President Donald Trump will deny the results of the midterm elections if Democrats take control of the House or Senate and warned the president could interfere with the results by using the same tactics he used in the aftermath of the 2020 presidential election.

“All it takes is for the president to say ‘The election was corrupt, and you need to go to the Capitol to fight, fight, fight,’” Himes said on the latest episode of the On NOTUS podcast. “This time it'll be you need to show up at polling places in Michigan and North Carolina and Georgia.”

“Don't tell me this is not possible, we saw what was possible on Jan. 6,” Himes said.

Himes, the ranking member on the House Intelligence Committee, said his Democratic colleagues are mobilizing ahead of the election, including running tabletop exercises for potential scenarios under the supervision of the House Administration Committee ranking member, Rep. Joe Morelle.

“It's not the Democrats' job to make sure that our elections are not compromised,” Himes said. “It's the American people's job, it's civil society. But obviously, since we know that it will be weaponized against us, we're very, very active on this right now.”
https://www.tiktok.com/@notusreports/video/7665310109991505165Himes said Americans must do their own research about Trump’s false claims on foreign interference in elections for the good of American democracy.

“If an individual citizen can't exercise the critical faculties involved in seeing the president's lies for what they are, if 50% of America believes lies that are easily disprovable, we're done,” Himes said, adding that he wasn’t pessimistic about voters. “The real obligation lies with the American citizens.”

Himes’ warning comes days after Trump claimed vulnerabilities in America’s election system during a primetime address Himes said was a “pratfall.”

“It was a big nothing burger, pretty much everybody acknowledged that,” Himes said. “I've looked at all the intelligence and, by the way, you don't need to trust me, you can go look at the… intelligence community assessment around the election of 2020.”

Himes also urged Congress to reauthorize Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, a controversial surveillance tool that lets the federal government collect communications of foreigners overseas.

“Congress doesn't act very well unless the unabstract pain of not acting is right in your face,” Himes said. “Heaven forbid, but if we had an attack because 702 didn't allow us to follow, connect the dots, all of a sudden we'd get called back here and 702 would be passed in a millisecond.”

Authorization for Section 702 expired in June, but Himes said it is still operational while companies continue to cooperate with government requests.

Himes said that he was “pained” by Director of National Intelligence nominee Jay Clayton’s testimony at his confirmation hearing before the Senate Intelligence Committee, but said he expected Clayton to be “law-oriented” and a better choice than the acting DNI head, Bill Pulte.

“Bill Pulte has shown that he will very happily break the law,” Himes said. “Choose Jay Clayton every single day and twice on Sunday, in terms of the likelihood that that individual is gonna be profoundly corrupted.”

Himes brushed aside questions of division inside the Democratic Party over Israel and socialism by praising his party’s “big tent” and the potential success it could yield at the ballot box.

“You don't need to be a mathematical genius to know that the party that gets the biggest tent, that has the most people in it, is going to have majorities in the House and the Senate and probably win the presidency,” Himes said. “That's just third-grade math.”

Still, Himes urged his fellow Democrats to avoid vilifying the ultra-rich and other groups while pushing for increased taxation.

“When you start getting into the business of vilifying billionaires, there's not that many billionaires, but now all of a sudden if you're vilifying corporations and the management class, and you're vilifying white men because they're toxic, pretty soon you're vilifying a good chunk of the American population that you desperately want supporting you,” Himes said.

On NOTUS is a weekly podcast where NOTUS reporters talk to lawmakers about their work in Washington and what motivates them. You can download or listen here.
